owner_answer.label: What we can say about noise
owner_answer.text: We measured battle luck by replaying each of the 40 starting teams three more times with nothing changed, 384 battles each time, and comparing every replay with the team's first score. Two scores of the same unchanged team differ by 3.40 win-rate points for tournament-ready teams and 3.73 points for search-found teams, root mean square, which is close to the 3.61 points that coin-flip arithmetic predicts for two independent scores near a 0.5 win rate over 384 battles. That luck is almost as large as the edits themselves, since a whole-Pokemon swap moved a tournament-ready team by 6.81 points before the correction and 5.90 points after it. We removed the luck by subtracting the replays' mean squared change from the edits' mean squared change and taking the square root, because a real change and independent luck add as squares. The correction works only on average over many edits, so it cannot say which single edit was real, and it cannot widen the measurement beyond one behaviour cloning policy against one pool of 50 opponent teams. It also floors a size at zero, which pushes small sizes upward, and every team scored on the same seed met the same opponent order and the same slot shuffles, so part of the luck is shared between teams.

candidates.sentence: We chose to replay every starting team three times with nothing changed over trusting the textbook formula for coin-flip noise, because the replays measure the luck of this exact setup. They agreed with the formula. Two scores of the same team differ by 3.40 win-rate points for tournament-ready teams, and the formula predicts 3.61.

facts.claim: Each of the 40 starting teams was replayed three times with nothing changed, on seeds 202, 303 and 404, 384 battles per score.
facts.source: code/docs/ruggedness2.md, Rerun with shuffled slots against the full meta, What stays

facts.claim: A replay is compared with the team's first score, the same reference the edits are compared with.

Two scores of the same unchanged team differ by 3.40 points for tournament-ready teams and 3.73 points for search-found teams, root mean square. Recomputed today from the saved scores: 3.404 and 3.726.
facts.source: v2/FACTS.md, Noise; code/docs/top50-one-edit.md, Noise floor; ~/vgc-data/edit_kind_rerun/run/results/ruggedness_shuffled50.json and ruggedness2_shuffled50_parts/vgc_battles.json

facts.claim: One score near 0.5 over 384 battles has a standard error of sqrt(0.25 / 384) = 2.55 points. The difference of two independent such scores has 2.55 times sqrt(2) = 3.61 points. The measured 3.40 and 3.73 sit on either side of 3.61, so battle luck behaves about like independent coin flips. The tournament-ready teams' mean first score was 0.507 and the search-found teams' 0.445, both close enough to 0.5 for this check.
facts.source: Arithmetic checked in python3 today; code/docs/top50-one-edit.md, Noise floor, for 2.55

candidates.sentence: We chose to subtract the replays' squared change from the edits' squared change over reading the raw change, because luck and a real change add as squares, so the raw number overstates every edit. A whole-Pokemon swap moved tournament-ready teams by 6.81 win-rate points before the correction and 5.90 after it. A stat alignment edit shrank from 3.92 to 1.95.

facts.claim: The size of an edit kind is the square root of the edits' mean squared change minus the replays' mean squared change, floored at zero: signal = max(edits - replays, 0.0), size = sqrt(signal).
facts.source: code/scripts/top50_one_edit.py, functions squared_moves and edit_size; same formula in ~/vgc-data/edit_kind_rerun/run/scripts/ruggedness2.py line 175 to 178

facts.claim: Why squares: a measured move is the real move plus battle noise, the two are independent, so their variances add. A replay is the same measurement with a real move of zero.

Tournament-ready teams, before and after the correction, in points: whole Pokemon 6.81 to 5.90, move 5.92 to 4.84, item 5.52 to 4.35, ability 5.00 to 3.66, stat alignment 3.92 to 1.95, Stat Points 3.76 to 1.60. The corrected values match FACTS.md.
facts.source: Recomputed today with python3 from ~/vgc-data/edit_kind_rerun/run/results, applying squared_moves to the saved scores

facts.claim: The correction assumes an edited team is about as noisy as its starting team, which holds while both win rates are near 0.5.

candidates.sentence: We chose to show the corrected sizes with their limits over presenting them as clean numbers, because the correction leaves three things a reader should still doubt. It removes luck only on average, so it cannot tell which single edit was real. It floors a size at zero, which pushes the small sizes upward. And every team scored on the same seed met the same opponents in the same order with the same slot shuffles, so part of the luck is shared between teams rather than independent.

facts.claim: The correction is computed from means over all edits of a kind and all replays of a group, so it has no per-edit reading.

The size is floored at zero with max(edits - replays, 0.0). The search-found stat alignment edits came out below the replays, minus 0.39 squared points, and are reported as 0.00. Several intervals have a lower end of exactly 0.
facts.source: code/scripts/top50_one_edit.py, function edit_size; recomputed today from the saved scores; v2/FACTS.md, size table

facts.claim: Every score on one seed uses the same fixed opponent schedule, the same seed for the team's own slot shuffle, seed plus one for the opponents' slot shuffle, and the same reseed of the battle random number generators. So all teams on seed 101 meet the same opponent sequence and the same shuffle sequence.
facts.source: /tmp/vgc-pilot/src/shard.py, function score_one and class ScheduledTeamBuilder; /tmp/vgc-pilot/src/slot_order.py, ShuffledTeamBuilder; scorer passes opp_schedule and seed in ~/vgc-data/edit_kind_rerun/run/scripts/ruggedness2.py line 131

facts.claim: Sign of shared luck in the data: the 16 search-found teams' replays averaged 1.78 points above their first scores, a t statistic of 2.6, where independent luck would centre on zero. The tournament-ready teams' replays averaged 0.59 points below, a t statistic of 1.0.
facts.source: Recomputed today with python3 from ruggedness2_shuffled50_parts/vgc_battles.json and ruggedness_shuffled50.json

facts.claim: Replay noise differed between replay seeds. Tournament-ready teams: 3.31, 3.34 and 3.56 points on seeds 202, 303 and 404. Search-found teams: 3.44, 2.79 and 4.70 points.
facts.source: Recomputed today with python3 from the saved replay scores

gaps: Does the post give the coin-flip prediction of 3.61 points beside the measured 3.40 and 3.73, or only the measured numbers?

Shared luck is confirmed in the code, and the search-found replays sit 1.78 points above their first scores on average. My reading, not measured: a shift shared by a whole seed hits the edits and the replays alike, since both are compared with the seed 101 score, so the subtraction should mostly cancel it. The bigger cost is that the bootstrap treats teams as independent, so the intervals may be too narrow. Do you want this caveat in the post, or only in the notes?
The top-50 study, issue #317, keeps the same seed design and has not started. Should it give each team its own seeds before it runs, so luck is not shared between teams?

Replay noise ranged from 2.79 to 4.70 points across seeds for the 16 search-found teams. I did not test whether that spread is more than chance for 16 teams. My rough estimate says it is within chance. Is that worth a check before the post goes out?
Which word does the reader see: battle luck, noise, or both with one defined by the other?
applied: Rami's note asked what we can say about noise, so I answered it in six sentences from the edit-kind rerun and checked each number against the code and the saved scores. I dropped the older panel design from 06-design-decisions.json and wrote three candidates on the replays, the squared subtraction, and the limits that remain, each limit confirmed in code or data.
